title: Experiment Design Under Real-World Pressure
description: Practice navigating advanced A/B testing decisions involving statistical rigor, experiment pitfalls, and strategic tradeoffs.

interactions.prompt: Spotify tests a new playlist algorithm. After 3 days on a 14-day test, variant B shows +12% engagement (p=0.03). Control had a known seasonal dip yesterday. What's the key concern?

options.text: The p-value is too low to be believable
Peeking at results early inflates false positive rate
Sample size is always sufficient after 3 days
Seasonal effects and early stopping both threaten validity

chartData.title: Engagement Rate: Control vs Variant B (Days 1-3)

interactions.prompt: Your e-commerce team can run one experiment this quarter. Option A: test a checkout redesign (high revenue impact, 8-week runtime needed). Option B: test homepage banner copy (lower impact, 2-week runtime, frees capacity for 3 more tests). Revenue targets are aggressive.

options.text: Run the checkout redesign — maximize expected revenue impact
Run the banner test and use remaining time for more experiments
Run both simultaneously to save time
Skip testing and ship the checkout redesign based on UX research

interactions.prompt: When multiple metrics are tested in one experiment, the probability of at least one false positive increases — this is called the ____ problem.

options.text: Multiple comparisons
Simpson's paradox
Selection bias
Regression to the mean

interactions.prompt: Airbnb's pricing experiment shows: Variant A lifts booking rate by +5% (p=0.04) but average revenue per booking drops -3% (p=0.09). Control: 10% booking rate, $150 avg booking. What matters most?

options.text: Booking rate is significant so ship Variant A immediately
Neither metric is significant enough to act on
Evaluate net revenue impact — the composite metric drives the decision
The revenue drop isn't significant so it can be ignored

chartData.title: A/B Test Results: Variant A vs Control

interactions.prompt: Rank these steps for designing a rigorous A/B test from FIRST to LAST: (a) Calculate required sample size, (b) Define primary metric and hypothesis, (c) Decide on significance threshold and power, (d) Launch experiment and monitor guardrail metrics.

options.text: Calculate required sample size
Define primary metric and hypothesis
Decide on significance threshold and power
Launch experiment and monitor guardrail metrics

interactions.prompt: DoorDash runs a delivery fee experiment. At 80% power, you need 4 weeks. Leadership wants results in 2 weeks. You can either reduce minimum detectable effect from 2% to 5%, or switch to a less precise proxy metric with faster signal. Which tradeoff do you accept?

options.text: Accept larger MDE — only detect big effects but keep true metric
Switch to proxy metric for speed and validate later
Run for 2 weeks and accept low power on original design
Push back on leadership and insist on 4 weeks

interactions.prompt: An A/B test concluded with p=0.048 and a 3% conversion lift. Rank these post-analysis checks from MOST to LEAST critical: (a) Check for sample ratio mismatch, (b) Segment results by device type, (c) Verify no overlapping experiments contaminated results, (d) Compute confidence interval width around the effect.

options.text: Check for sample ratio mismatch
Segment results by device type
Verify no overlapping experiment contamination
Compute confidence interval width around effect size

interactions.prompt: Post-launch monitoring reveals the winning variant's lift has decayed from +5% to +1.2% over 4 weeks. Power users adapted quickly but new users still show a +4.8% lift. How should you respond?

options.text: Roll back — the novelty effect invalidates the experiment entirely
Keep the variant but redesign for power user engagement separately
Ignore the decay — the original test was statistically valid
Rerun the full experiment from scratch with longer duration

interactions.priorContext: You previously shipped a winning A/B test variant for Netflix's recommendation UI with a +5% watch-time lift at p=0.02 after a properly powered 3-week experiment. Now real-world performance is diverging from test results.
